title: SHE WAS NO LONGER BEGGING TO BE LOVED—SHE KNEW SHE WAS DESIRED. AND THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING.
paragraphs: SHE WAS NO LONGER BEGGING TO BE LOVED—SHE KNEW SHE WAS DESIRED. AND THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING.

“I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.” — Song of Songs 7:10. One of Scripture’s most breathtaking declarations comes from a woman who is not pleading to be chosen, competing for affection, or apologizing for being loved. But what happens when a heart that has spent years feeling unwanted finally learns what it means to be cherished?
There is something almost shocking about the confidence in her voice.
She doesn't ask, “Am I beautiful enough?”
She doesn't whisper, “Do you still want me?”
She doesn't compare herself to another woman, search for reassurance, or prepare herself for the possibility of rejection.
She simply says:
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.” — Song of Songs 7:10 (KJV)
Read that again.
Not because it is a pretty verse to put on a wedding photograph.
Not because it sounds romantic.
But because some people have spent their entire lives trying to believe that they could be loved without constantly proving they deserve it.
And here stands a woman who speaks as though she has nothing left to prove.
She knows whose she is.
She knows she is wanted.
And she is not ashamed to say it.
But before we turn her words into another inspirational slogan, we need to understand what Scripture is actually saying.
Because the truth is more beautiful when we stop forcing the Bible to say what we wish it said and allow it to speak for itself.
In the original Hebrew, Song of Songs 7:10 reads:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani le-dodi, ve'alai teshuqato.
A faithful rendering is:
“I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me.”
The Hebrew word דּוֹדִי (dodi) means “my beloved,” an affectionate expression used throughout the Song.
The word תְּשׁוּקָה (teshuqah) means “desire” or “longing.”
It is not a casual word.
It appears in only three verses in the Hebrew Bible: Genesis 3:16, Genesis 4:7, and Song of Songs 7:10.
Its meaning must be understood within each passage rather than assuming it always describes the same kind of desire.

In Genesis 3:16, it appears in the painful consequences of humanity's fall. In Genesis 4:7, it describes sin's desire directed toward Cain. But here, in the poetry of Song of Songs, it belongs to the language of romantic longing.
A woman speaks of her beloved's desire for her.
And the remarkable thing is that she speaks without embarrassment.
There is no shame attached to being desired within this celebration of love.
No suggestion that her womanhood makes her less worthy of honor.
No indication that her voice should be silenced because she expresses delight in being wanted.
She is not merely the object of another person's affection.
She is a speaking, choosing, responding participant in love.
And that matters.
Because somewhere along the way, many people learned to confuse being desired with being valued.
Some learned that attention meant love.
That jealousy meant devotion.
That physical attraction meant commitment.
That being pursued meant being protected.
And some discovered, painfully, that a person can desire your body without honoring your soul.
Someone can want your attention without wanting your well-being.
Someone can promise forever while having no intention of remaining faithful tomorrow.
Perhaps you know that pain.
Perhaps you once believed that if somebody wanted you badly enough, they would never leave.
But they did.
Perhaps you gave everything you knew how to give, believing that sacrifice would finally make you irreplaceable.
And still, you were abandoned.
Perhaps you stayed in a relationship long after love had been replaced by fear, because being unwanted seemed more terrifying than being mistreated.
Or perhaps nobody ever broke your heart in a dramatic way.
Perhaps the wound was quieter.
A childhood where affection felt conditional.
A marriage where tenderness slowly disappeared.
Years of being compared to somebody prettier, younger, more successful, or more impressive.
A lifetime of smiling when people complimented you, while secretly wondering what they would think if they knew the things you regretted.
And now, when someone tells you that you are loved, a part of you still asks:
“For how long?”
That is why this woman's confidence can feel almost unfamiliar.
She is not negotiating for affection. She is resting in a relationship where desire is openly expressed.
But we must be careful here.
Song of Songs is first and foremost biblical love poetry celebrating the affection, attraction, commitment, and mutual delight of human lovers.
It is not originally a sentence spoken directly by Jesus to every individual believer.
The woman is speaking about her beloved within the poem.
And honoring that original meaning does not make the passage less spiritual.
It makes our understanding more faithful.
The Bible does not need us to erase human love to make it holy.
God created human beings with bodies, emotions, affection, and the capacity for covenantal intimacy.
Genesis 2:25 describes the man and his wife as naked and unashamed before sin entered the world.
The Song celebrates something deeply human: the goodness of being known, cherished, and welcomed by someone who loves you.
It also refuses to portray the woman as voiceless.
Earlier, she declares:
“My beloved is mine, and I am his.” — Song of Songs 2:16 (KJV)
Later:
“I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine.” — Song of Songs 6:3 (KJV)
And finally:
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.” — Song of Songs 7:10 (KJV)
Notice how the language develops.
The first declaration celebrates mutual belonging.
The second begins with her belonging to her beloved.
The third emphasizes that belonging and his desire for her.
We should not pretend that this poetic progression gives us a complete psychological history of the woman. Scripture does not tell us that she overcame abandonment, insecurity, or a traumatic past.
But her words do reveal a confidence worth contemplating.
She is able to receive love without treating her beloved's desire as something shameful.
And for someone who has lived under rejection, even imagining that kind of confidence can be difficult.
Because rejection has a way of becoming a voice.
At first, it sounds like something another person said.
Then, after enough time, it begins to sound like your own thoughts.
“You're too damaged.”
“You're not attractive enough.”
“You have too much history.”
“Nobody would choose you if they knew everything.”
And sometimes the cruelest voice is not the person who hurt you.
It is the voice you carried home after they left.
You begin to rehearse the rejection.
You study yourself for flaws.
You wonder whether being thinner, quieter, stronger, more successful, less emotional, or more accommodating would have changed the outcome.
Eventually, you may stop asking whether someone loves you.
You start asking whether you are even lovable.
And this is where we must move carefully from the Song's celebration of human love to the greater testimony of Scripture concerning God's redeeming love.
Not by pretending that the beloved in Song of Songs 7:10 is explicitly Jesus.
But by allowing the whole Bible to lead us to the One who reveals the fullness of divine love.
Jesus Christ.
The One who did not merely speak about love from a safe distance.
The One who entered a world of betrayal, humiliation, violence, and death.
The One who knew what it was to be despised and rejected.
Isaiah 53:3 calls the suffering servant “despised and rejected of men” (KJV), a passage Christians understand in light of Christ's suffering.
Jesus understands rejection.
Not as an abstract concept.
He was betrayed by Judas.
Denied by Peter.
Abandoned by His disciples when He was arrested.
Mocked by soldiers.
Condemned before a crowd.
Crucified outside the city.
And yet, the Gospel tells us something extraordinary.
His love was not defeated by the hatred directed toward Him.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we learned how to appear religious.
Not after we made our past disappear.
Not after we became impressive enough to deserve salvation.
While we were yet sinners.
The Greek word translated “commendeth” is συνίστησιν (synistēsin), which in this context conveys that God demonstrates or shows His love.
God's love is not presented merely as a feeling He claims to have.
It is demonstrated in the death of Christ.
And the word ἁμαρτωλῶν (hamartōlōn) means “sinners.”
Paul does not describe people who had already made themselves righteous.
He describes the very people for whom Christ gave His life.
That is the scandal of grace.
The holy Son of God died for the ungodly.
The innocent suffered for the guilty.
The One without sin bore the judgment our sin deserved.
And He did not do it because sin was insignificant.
He did it because sin was so serious that redemption required the cross, and because God's mercy is greater than anything we could earn.
Please understand the difference.
The Gospel does not say that everything you have ever done was acceptable.
It says that Jesus Christ is mighty to save sinners who cannot save themselves.
It does not tell you to celebrate your rebellion.
It calls you to repent and believe.
It does not tell you that your wounds are imaginary.
It tells you that your wounds do not place you beyond the reach of God's mercy.
And it does not promise that every person who rejected you will eventually recognize your worth.
It points you to a Savior whose faithfulness does not depend on human approval.
There is a woman in John chapter 4 whose story makes this painfully real.
She comes to a well.
Jesus is there.
He asks her for a drink.
And what follows is one of the most remarkable conversations recorded in the Gospels.
She is a Samaritan woman, and Jesus is a Jewish man. Their interaction crosses deeply rooted social and religious divisions.
Jesus speaks to her about living water.
He knows the truth about her life.
He tells her that she has had five husbands and that the man she currently has is not her husband.
Scripture does not explain why those marriages ended, so we must not invent a history of promiscuity, abandonment, or moral failure for every relationship she experienced.
But the text does reveal that Jesus knows intimate details about her circumstances.
And He continues speaking with her.
He does not pretend that truth is unnecessary.
He does not avoid the difficult conversation.
But neither does He treat her as someone unworthy of hearing about the gift of God.
He reveals profound truths about worship.
And when she speaks about the coming Messiah, Jesus tells her:
“I that speak unto thee am he.” — John 4:26 (KJV)
Think about that.
A woman whose life was known to Him hears Jesus identify Himself as the Messiah.
She then leaves her waterpot, goes into the city, and tells the people:
“Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?” — John 4:29 (KJV)
And many Samaritans believe because of her testimony.
She came to the well for water.
She encountered the Messiah.
And she became a witness.
The beauty is not that Jesus ignored the truth about her life.
The beauty is that the truth about her life did not prevent Him from speaking to her about salvation.
Somebody reading this needs that distinction.
Because you have been hiding from God as though He would discover something shocking if you finally told Him the truth.
But He already knows.
He knows what you did.
He knows what was done to you.
He knows the decisions you regret and the circumstances you never chose.
He knows the prayers you stopped praying.
He knows the bitterness you have been feeding.
He knows the relationship you keep returning to, even though it is pulling you away from obedience.
He knows the shame you carry into church beneath a carefully arranged smile.
And the Gospel invitation remains:
Repent.
Believe in Jesus Christ.
Come into the light.
Not because darkness was harmless.
But because Christ came to rescue sinners from darkness.
There is another woman in Luke chapter 7.
She enters a Pharisee's house while Jesus is eating.
She weeps at His feet.
Her tears fall upon them.
She wipes them with her hair, kisses His feet, and anoints them with ointment.
The Pharisee sees a woman known as a sinner.
Jesus sees her actions of love and addresses the deeper issue of forgiveness.
He tells her:
“Thy sins are forgiven.” — Luke 7:48 (KJV)
And then:
“Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.” — Luke 7:50 (KJV)
Not “Your beauty saved you.”
Not “Your usefulness saved you.”
Not “Your ability to impress religious people saved you.”
Your faith has saved you.
She is not saved by becoming desirable in the eyes of the crowd.
She receives forgiveness through faith.
And that is where the Gospel corrects something dangerous in the way we sometimes talk about being loved.
Your deepest need is not to become the person everybody wants.
Your deepest need is to be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Human desire, even when genuine and honorable, cannot carry the weight of your eternal identity.
A husband cannot be your savior.
A wife cannot be your savior.
A boyfriend, girlfriend, admirer, or future spouse cannot cleanse your conscience, forgive your sins, or conquer death.
Only Christ can do that.
And this is why the Christian hope is so much greater than the promise of romance.
The Song of Songs gives us a beautiful picture of human love.
The Gospel gives us the saving revelation of God's love in Jesus Christ.
We should treasure both without confusing them.
Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” (KJV)
Notice the direction of the comparison.
Christ's self-giving love becomes the standard by which husbands are commanded to love their wives.
Paul then describes marriage as a profound mystery in relation to Christ and the church.
Here, Scripture itself establishes a connection between covenant marriage and Christ's relationship with His people.
But Christ's love is not reducible to romantic attraction.
His love is holy.
Sacrificial.
Faithful.
Redemptive.
He gave Himself to sanctify His people.
He does not simply affirm us in everything we are.
He saves us and transforms us.
That means you do not have to spend the rest of your life begging human beings to give you the identity that belongs to you in Christ.
If you belong to Jesus through faith, you are not spiritually abandoned.
You have been brought near by His blood.
You have been adopted into God's family.
You are called to walk in the newness of life that His grace makes possible.
And that identity remains meaningful whether you are married, single, widowed, divorced, waiting, grieving, or rebuilding.
Being unmarried does not mean you are undesired by God.
Being rejected by a person does not mean God has rejected you.
Being physically scarred, aging, ill, or unable to meet the world's beauty standards does not make you less human or less worthy of dignity.
Your value does not expire when someone stops finding you attractive.
And your standing before God is not established by how many people choose you.
It is established through Jesus Christ, received by grace through faith.
Perhaps that is where this message becomes personal.
Because there are people who know the language of grace but still live as prisoners of rejection.
They sing about God's love on Sunday.
Then spend Monday measuring themselves against someone else's appearance, achievements, marriage, or success.
They tell others that Jesus is enough.
Then quietly wonder whether they will ever feel enough.
And sometimes their insecurity leads them into places they never imagined they would go.
They tolerate dishonesty because they fear loneliness.
They compromise convictions because they fear being abandoned.
They keep answering messages from people who repeatedly hurt them.
They confuse being pursued with being cherished.
They mistake possession for protection.
And when the relationship finally collapses, they conclude that they were the problem.
But listen carefully.
Being wanted is not the same as being loved well.
Real love does not require you to surrender your conscience to keep someone's attention.
Real love does not celebrate what destroys you.
Real love is not proven by manipulation, coercion, or the threat of abandonment.
First Corinthians 13 describes love as patient and kind, refusing to rejoice in wrongdoing and rejoicing instead in truth.
The Bible's vision of love includes faithfulness, responsibility, honor, and holiness.
And the woman in Song of Songs 7:10 is not giving anyone permission to treat desire as an excuse for selfishness.
She is expressing confidence in the love celebrated by the poem.
There is dignity in that.
There is freedom in being able to say, without boasting or fear, that you are cherished.
But perhaps today you cannot say those words about another human being.
Perhaps your marriage is struggling.
Perhaps your spouse has died.
Perhaps you have never experienced a safe and faithful relationship.
Perhaps you are recovering from betrayal.
Perhaps you are single and weary of hearing that your life will finally begin when someone chooses you.
Then hear this:
Your life is not on hold until romance arrives.
Your purpose is not incomplete because you do not have a wedding ring.
Your calling is not less meaningful because nobody is holding your hand.
Jesus Christ Himself lived a fully human, perfectly obedient life without marrying.
The apostle Paul taught that singleness can be a meaningful calling in service to the Lord.
So never allow anyone to use Song of Songs 7:10 to make you believe that romantic desire is the highest proof of your worth.
It isn't.
The highest revelation of God's saving love is found at the cross and in the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And if you are married, let this verse challenge you in another way.
When was the last time your spouse felt genuinely cherished?
Not merely needed.
Not merely tolerated.
Not merely useful for paying bills, raising children, preparing meals, or keeping the household together.
Cherished.
When was the last time you expressed affection without demanding something in return?
When was the last time you listened without preparing your defense?
When was the last time you remembered that the person beside you is not an accessory to your life but someone made in the image of God?
Desire within marriage should never become an excuse for entitlement.
It should be joined to tenderness, mutual honor, patience, and faithful love.
A relationship in which someone can confidently say, “I am loved,” is not built by beautiful words alone.
It is nurtured through consistent acts of care.
And perhaps there is repentance needed here.
Perhaps you have been careless with someone else's heart.
Perhaps you have withheld affection as punishment.
Perhaps you have made someone feel invisible while insisting that your intentions were good.
Perhaps you have pursued admiration from strangers while neglecting the person to whom you made promises.
If the Holy Spirit is bringing something to light, do not silence that conviction.
Confess what is wrong.
Turn away from it.
Seek forgiveness.
And where harm has been done, take responsibility through meaningful change rather than demanding instant trust.
Grace is not permission to continue hurting people.
Grace calls us into a new way of living.
And if you are the one who has been wounded, forgiveness does not mean pretending that abuse is love or that trust must be restored without safety and accountability.
God does not command you to call evil good.
You can pursue healing, seek wise help, and establish necessary boundaries while entrusting your life to Christ.
There is something deeply moving about a woman who can speak of love without fear.
But there is something even more astonishing about a sinner who can stand before God without condemnation because of Jesus.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
No condemnation.
Not because they never sinned.
Not because their past was imaginary.
Not because God decided holiness no longer mattered.
But because Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He bore our sin.
He died.
He rose again.
And those who belong to Him are justified by grace through faith.
That is the foundation beneath the confidence of a redeemed soul.
Not arrogance.
Not self-worship.
Not pretending to be flawless.
But trusting the Savior who is sufficient.
And perhaps the most important question today is not whether someone desires you.
Perhaps it is whether you have surrendered your life to the One who died and rose again to save sinners.
Have you trusted Jesus Christ?
Have you repented of your sin?
Are you following Him, or merely collecting religious words that make you feel better for a moment?
Because it is possible to admire grace without receiving it.
It is possible to share Bible verses while refusing to obey the Lord.
It is possible to crave the comfort of being loved while resisting the transformation that God's love produces.
Jesus did not die merely to improve your self-image.
He died to redeem you.
To reconcile you to God.
To make you His own.
To give you new life.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
This is not a promise that every painful memory instantly disappears.
It is a declaration of the new reality of belonging to Christ.
The past no longer has the authority to define your standing before God.
Sin no longer has the right to be your master.
Shame does not have the final word.
Jesus does.
And His resurrection means that even death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is why our message has always been:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because He calls sin righteousness.
Not because He erases every earthly consequence of our choices.
But because His grace can redeem people whose stories seem beyond repair.
Peter denied Him.
Yet the risen Christ restored Peter to service.
Paul persecuted the church.
Yet the grace of God transformed him into a witness for the very Savior he had opposed.
The Samaritan woman encountered Jesus and testified to her neighbors.
The sinful woman in Luke 7 heard words of forgiveness and peace.
Different lives.
Different circumstances.
One glorious truth.
Jesus Christ is able to save.
And He is still worthy of your trust today.
Maybe you are reading this late at night.
The house is quiet.
Your phone is in your hand.
Everybody thinks you are doing fine.
But you know how many times you have cried over the same wound.
You know how often you have wondered whether God could still use someone with your history.
You know how exhausted you are from pretending that rejection did not change you.
You have learned how to smile before people notice the sadness.
You have learned how to say, “I'm okay,” before anyone asks a second question.
But what if tonight you stopped pretending?
What if you brought the truth into the presence of Christ?
Not a polished version of yourself.
Not the version that knows all the correct Christian phrases.
The real you.
The one who is tired.
The one who is ashamed.
The one who still struggles.
The one who needs mercy.
You do not need to convince Jesus that your wounds are worth noticing.
You need to come to Him in faith.
And if you have wandered from Him, return.
If you have been living in sin, repent.
If you have placed your identity in another person's approval, surrender that idol.
If you have allowed bitterness to rule your heart, bring it before the Lord.
If you have confused God's patience with permission to disobey, do not delay.
His mercy is not an invitation to remain unchanged.
It is an invitation to come home.
And if you cannot find the words, perhaps begin here:

“Lord Jesus, You know everything about me. You know my sins, my wounds, my fears, and the things I have tried to hide. I confess that I need Your mercy. Forgive me. Teach me to repent sincerely, trust Your finished work, and follow You in obedience. Heal what has been wounded, correct what has been sinful, and shape my heart according to Your Word. I do not want to build my identity on human approval anymore. I want to belong to You. Amen.”
There is no magic in repeating a prayer.
Salvation is not earned by saying the correct words.
It is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
But a sincere prayer can be the beginning of an honest response to His Gospel.
And if this message has reached a place in your heart that you have been hiding for years, do not let the moment pass without reflection.
You do not have to publish the details of your pain to be worthy of prayer.
Someone else may need to hear that the grace of God is not merely something we talk about.
It is something that changes lives.
Please also think of one person who needs this message.
A friend who keeps returning to a relationship that is destroying their peace.
A mother who feels invisible.
A husband who has forgotten how to express tenderness.
A young woman who thinks her worth depends on her appearance.
A single believer who has begun to believe that being unmarried means being unwanted.
A person who has stopped going to church because shame convinced them that God would never welcome them.
Not merely to increase the reach of a page.
But because the truth of Scripture deserves to travel farther than the walls of a church building.
They may never ask anyone for spiritual help.
They may never tell you how deeply they are hurting.
But they might read an article that you share.
And through that simple act, they may encounter the message of Christ's forgiveness and the hope of His Gospel.
One faithful share cannot save a soul. Only Jesus saves. But God can use an ordinary act of sharing to bring His Word before someone who needs to hear it.

Not as a substitute for opening your Bible, but as a reminder to return to these passages, examine their context, and let Scripture reshape the way you understand love, dignity, repentance, and grace.

And if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand the Bible more deeply, consider following our page and inviting your family, friends, fellow believers, seekers, and even those who are skeptical of Christianity to follow along.
We want people to encounter more than emotional words.
We want them to encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
Scripture that can be examined.
Grace that does not excuse sin.
Conviction that leads toward repentance.
Encouragement that does not depend on pretending life is easy.
And discipleship that continues after the emotion of a single article has faded.
Because there is a difference between reading a message that encourages you today and helping make Scripture-centered encouragement available to others tomorrow.
It can be a voluntary expression of generosity and support for Gospel outreach.
But we want to be clear about something important.
The biblical principle of giving is not about pressuring people into financial commitments to prove their love for Jesus.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
Giving should be willing.
Thoughtful.
Faithful.
Free from manipulation.
Your responsibilities to your family, your local church, and those genuinely in need matter.
If you cannot, you are still welcome here.
You can pray.
You can read.
You can share.
You can encourage others.
You can grow in Christ.
And none of those things makes you a second-class member of the Christian community.
We also want to express our appreciation in a practical way.
These are simply thank-you benefits for supporters, not measures of anyone's spiritual maturity or standing before God.
We want believers to have access to resources that encourage serious Bible study, prayer, spiritual growth, sound doctrine, and a deeper walk with Jesus Christ.
Our prayer is that these resources will help people move beyond momentary inspiration into a life increasingly shaped by God's Word.
Because a powerful article may move you today.
But faithful discipleship is about following Jesus tomorrow.
And the next day.
And through the seasons when obedience is difficult, prayers feel unanswered, and the excitement of a spiritual moment has become the quiet work of trusting God.
That Christ would be glorified.
That sinners would hear the Gospel.
That believers would be strengthened.
That the wounded would find faithful care.
That the wandering would be called to repentance.
And that more people would discover the grace of God revealed in Jesus Christ.
Now, before you leave, return with me to the woman in Song of Songs.
Listen to her voice one more time.
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.”
There is no frantic bargaining in her words.
No desperate attempt to become someone else.
No apology for being cherished.
Just the beautiful confidence of a woman speaking within the love celebrated by the Song.
Perhaps that verse will inspire you to cherish your spouse more faithfully.
Perhaps it will remind you that human affection, rightly ordered, is a gift of God.
Perhaps it will challenge you to stop measuring your worth by people who never learned how to love you well.
But above all, let the whole testimony of Scripture draw you beyond even the most beautiful human relationship.
To Christ.
Because even the best earthly love cannot promise never to die.
Even the most devoted human heart cannot forgive your sins.
Even the strongest marriage cannot raise you from the grave.
But Jesus Christ died and rose again.
And through Him, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and given the hope of everlasting life.
So do not leave this message merely asking, “Does someone desire me?”
Ask something far more important.
“Do I belong to Jesus Christ?”
And if you do, by His grace through faith, then learn to live from that truth.
Not as someone who must constantly earn the right to exist.
Not as someone whose past is more powerful than the cross.
Not as someone whose future depends on the approval of people.
But as someone called to holiness, upheld by mercy, and invited to walk faithfully with the Savior.
You may still have tears to cry.
You may still have wounds that need time and care.
You may still be waiting for answers.
But you do not have to make rejection your identity.
You do not have to make shame your permanent home.
You do not have to keep returning to the chains from which Christ calls you to freedom.
There is repentance.
There is forgiveness.
There is grace.
There is a new life in Jesus Christ.
And there is hope beyond the final page of every earthly love story.
The hands that were pierced for your redemption are stronger than the voices that taught you to feel unwanted.
